in_text_mentions: Most children are asymptomatic in the early phase of ingestion. Symptoms progress according to the duration of ingestion and the location of the magnet. Symptoms are usually non-specific; however, vomiting and abdominal pain are the two most common symptoms (6–8). Most patients who present with vague abdominal pain are diagnosed with an abdominal radiograph (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: Laboratory investigations were normal except for a mild leukocytosis. An erect abdominal X-ray demonstrated the presence of five bullet-shaped magnets in the lower abdomen without air-fluid levels or air under the diaphragm (Fig. 1).Fig. 1An erect abdominal X-ray showing five bullet shaped magnets in the lower abdomen with no air-fluid levels or air under the diaphragm.Fig. 1

In the current case, 30 days passed after the ingestion, and only 2 magnets out of 7 passed. The remaining 5 magnets were obviously attached to each other on an abdominal X-ray (Fig. 1). Therefore, surgical exploration and removal of the remaining magnets to prevent potential complications, such as intestinal fistulae formation, and/or to address such complications was deemed the safest decision.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: The panel shows an endoscopic view of multiple magnets (11 magnets) clustered in the prepyloric gastric region, causing direct physical impingement and inflammation (erythema and congestion) on the gastric mucosa, which is a direct clinical manifestation of multiple magnet ingestion. B: The panel shows a second endoscopic view of the same cluster of magnets in the prepyloric gastric region, demonstrating the clinical consequence of multiple magnet ingestion: direct contact and pressure on the mucosal lining.
panels.attribution_text: Lorenze et al. Gastric Mucosa Fistula Secondary to Magnet Ingestion.. JPGN reports 2020. doi:10.1097/pg9.0000000000000015. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
in_text_mentions: firmed a radiopaque beaded density over the gastric body (Fig. 1). The patient had no vomiting or abdominal pain. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) using an Olympus gastroscope (GIF-H190) demonstrated a ring of 11 magnets pinching the gastric mucosa in the prepyloric region along the lesser curvature (Fig. 2). The mucosa appeared erythematous and congested at the contact site with the magnets. Multiple attempts at endoscopic removal with rat-toothed forceps and foreign body graspers were unsuccessful, and the procedure was aborted due to respiratory distress and concern for gastric perforation.

panels.rationale: The panel is a clinical abdominal radiograph of a patient (a child) clearly showing a linear chain of radiopaque foreign bodies (magnets), which is the definitive clinical presentation of multiple magnet ingestion.
panels.attribution_text: Areed et al. Multiple Magnet Ingestion in a Child With an Overlooked Diagnosis Leading to Intestinal Perforation.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.104994. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Abdominal radiograph in the erect position showing a well-defined chain of beaded magnets representing a foreign body (arrow)
in_text_mentions: Clinical exam revealed a soft abdomen without tenderness or guarding. Abdominal radiograph revealed a chain of radiopaque and rounded FBs in the lower abdomen (Figure 1). CT abdomen demonstrated a large, irregular FB within the distal ileum (Figure 2). Initial blood investigations were within normal range. Laparoscopy was planned for both diagnostic evaluation and definitive management.

in_text_mentions: After 72 hours, she was readmitted with the same complaint. An X-ray of the abdomen showed signs of intestinal obstruction (Figure 4), which was confirmed by an abdominal CT scan (Figure 5). The patient was booked for laparoscopic surgery, and it was found that there were dilated small bowel loops, with a band extending from the mid-ileum to the cecum and an enteroenteric fistula between the terminal ileum and cecum. The band was divided, and laparoscopic-assisted division of the fistula was performed and sutured (Figure 6).

panels.figure_caption: Left lateral decubitus radiograph obtained in a 5 year-old boy with the new complaint of abdominal pain the morning after an MRI of neck was performed for complaint of neck pain. Radiograph demonstrates 11 round metallic objects 4 mm in diameter and pneumoperitoneum.
in_text_mentions: g, but he was now complaining of severe abdominal pain and refusal to eat. Plain radiographs of the abdomen were obtained which demonstrated pneumoperitoneum and 11 small round metallic objects in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen (Figure 1). The pediatric general surgeon was consulted, and the child was taken to the operating room emergently for exploratory laparotomy. Intra-operatively, four 5–7 mm full thickness perforations to the small intestine were identified and primarily repaired. Eleven small spherical magnets measuring 4 mm in diameter were retrieved from within the peritoneum.
